svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. Port 443 is a destination, not a disguise
svg.desc: An explanation of why running a VPN protocol on the standard web port does not hide it. Inspection equipment looks at four things beyond the port number: the byte patterns in the opening handshake, which are distinctive per protocol; the client's own handshake fingerprint, which does not match any browser; the sizes and timing of packets, which do not resemble page loads; and the behaviour of the connection when probed. Published research in 2022 demonstrated identification of one protocol with high accuracy and low false positives, including flows using simple obfuscation. A band below explains where genuine obfuscation sits, that it is a separate layer rather than a port choice, and that it makes traffic unremarkable rather than unobservable.
svg.text: Figure 2: Port 443 Is a Destination, Not a Disguise
"Firewalls cannot block port 443 without blocking the whole web" is true, and it is not an argument that your traffic looks like the web.
The claim: run OpenVPN over TCP on port 443 and it is indistinguishable from HTTPS
This appears in nearly every protocol guide, including the one this lesson is built from, usually as the top recommendation for restrictive networks.
Inspection equipment has not worked that way for some years, and the research demonstrating it is now several years old.

svg.text: Where the real answer lives, and it is a separate layer rather than a port number
Obfuscation is a wrapper placed around a tunnel whose job is to remove exactly the four signals above: it randomises the handshake so there are no fixed opening
bytes, it makes the endpoint refuse to identify itself when probed, and in the better designs it reshapes packet sizes and timing.

g.text: Providers ship this under their own names. Look for a mode described as obfuscated, stealth, or bridge, rather than assuming a protocol choice covers it.
It is a different question from which protocol you use, and a provider may offer excellent protocols and no obfuscation at all. Check separately.

svg.text: And the caveat that the research itself insists on
Simple obfuscation, of the kind that scrambles the payload without changing the behaviour, was defeated in the same study. Anybody whose safety depends on their
tunnel being invisible should not assume it is. Obfuscation makes traffic unremarkable at scale. It does not make it unobservable to somebody looking at you.
So the honest advice is: pick the protocol on the other five rows of Figure 1, and treat censorship resistance as a separate feature you check for by name.
Port 443 remains useful for getting through a firewall that only filters by port. That is a different and much smaller claim than the one usually made for it.
